draft.title: Tests for ions
card: Flame test
A metal ion gives a flame a set colour when heated. Sodium gives yellow-orange, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper blue-green.
Precipitation test
Adding a solution that forms a solid with the ion you suspect shows if it is present. The solid is a precipitate, and its colour helps identify the ion.
Anion tests
Chloride gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate solution. Sulfate gives a white precipitate with barium nitrate solution. Carbonate fizzes with dilute acid, releasing carbon dioxide.
Ions can interfere with each other, so a test is chosen so that other ions in the sample do not give the same result. Dilute acid is often added first to remove carbonate.
draft.remember: Each ion gives its own sign: a flame colour, a precipitate or a gas.

a.q: A student adds silver nitrate solution to a clear solution, and a white precipitate forms. Which ion is the student testing for?
a.why: Silver nitrate gives a white precipitate with chloride ions. Sulfate is tested with barium nitrate, so it is the tempting wrong answer, since its precipitate is also white.
a.clue: Match the test solution to the ion it detects.

b.q: Sodium carbonate powder is added to dilute hydrochloric acid and it fizzes. Which result confirms the fizzing gas came from the carbonate ion?
opts: The solution is clear and colourless
A white precipitate forms with silver nitrate
b.why: Carbonate reacts with dilute acid to release carbon dioxide, so fizzing points to carbonate. The yellow-orange flame shows sodium, which is a metal ion and not the anion. The silver nitrate precipitate would come from the chloride in the hydrochloric acid, not the carbonate.
b.clue: Which result belongs to the anion, not the metal ion?

problems.detail: "Each ion gives its own sign" suggests every result is unique to one ion. The card says ions can interfere, and chloride and sulfate both give white precipitates, so the remember line contradicts the card.

The stem already names the powder as sodium carbonate, so asking which result confirms the gas came from carbonate is circular and may confuse students. It would be clearer as an unknown white powder.
The card says carbonate releases carbon dioxide but never says how a student would show the gas is carbon dioxide (for example, limewater turning milky).

check.summary: The facts are correct and both intended answers are right. The remember line overstates that each ion has a unique sign, against the card's point on interference, and question b names the carbonate in its stem, which makes it circular, without the card teaching how to identify carbon dioxide.

proposal.title: Tests for ions
card: Flame test
A metal ion gives a flame a set colour when heated. Sodium gives yellow-orange, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper blue-green.
Precipitation test

Adding a solution that forms a solid, called a precipitate, with the suspected ion shows if it is present. Chloride gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate, and sulfate gives a white precipitate with barium nitrate.
Carbonate test
Carbonate fizzes with dilute acid, releasing carbon dioxide gas. Bubbling the gas through limewater turns it milky, which confirms it is carbon dioxide.
Some ions give the same result, so they can interfere. Dilute nitric acid is often added first to remove carbonate, which would otherwise also form a precipitate.
proposal.remember: Match each test to the ion it detects, and remove interfering ions such as carbonate first.
